newsitem.title: ITALY: Italian metalworkers' dispute moves towards deal.
newsitem.headline: Italian metalworkers' dispute moves towards deal.

text.p: A protracted pay dispute in Italy's engineering and metalworking industry moved towards a settlement on Monday after the government presented a new proposal to unions and employers at all-night talks.
"The government's proposal broadly incorporates the positions...so I think it should be accepted," Labour Minister Tiziano Treu told Italian television.
He said he hoped an agreement could be signed within 24 hours "because all the main issues are covered".
Treu spoke following all-night talks between unions, employers and the government in the seven-month-old stand off.
The leader of metalworkers' union UILM, Luigi Angeletti, said he was optimistic that a deal was within reach.
"We will evaluate the merits of the proposal tomorrow and will give a final opinion. I am optimistic," Angeletti said.
UILM and the FIM and FIOM unions represent Italy's 1.7 million engineering and metalworkers in a sector which accounts for 40 percent of industrial output.
Any settlement is likely to set the tone for other pay accords and prove key to Italy's hopes of containing inflation.
The unions and employers' group Federmeccanica were expected to give their response to the government proposal by Tuesday.
Prime Minister Romano Prodi's government proposed a 30-month national contract period to replace a two-year contract which expired last June.
The employers would make a one-off payment of 512,000 lire ($316) paid in two instalments to cover the first six months.
It would be followed by graduated monthly wage increases totalling 200,000 lire ($124) during the rest of the contract, a government statement said.
Employers' association Confindustria refused to comment on the content of the proposal.

"We agreed with the government and the unions that we would not reveal our views on the contract, but I confirm that we share Federmeccanica's position," Confindustria's vice-president Carlo Caliieri said.
Shares in car giant Fiat, Italy's biggest company, extended gains on Monday amid optimism that a settlement would be signed.
Fiat shares were quoted up 2.1 percent at 5,245 ($3.23) at 1445 after hitting a day's high of 5,355 lire.
In December, Federmeccanica rejected a government proposal of a 200,000 lire wage increase as inflationary.
"The first government proposal was not inflationary and the new one is not," analyst Maria Rosa Trolese of Deutsche Bank said.
"The markets expected this kind of pay increase and do not fear it, especially after the Bank of Italy's cut in interest rates in January."
The central bank cut the discount rate to 6.75 percent from 7.50 percent on January 21 after a steady decline in inflation, now running at about 2.6 percent year-on-year.
